overview: The atlas calls this 1492 to 1530 region Papua New Guinea, but that modern state did not exist. The two imported polygons cover much of eastern New Guinea and a second island component while omitting Wewak, Madang, Milne Bay, the Trobriands, Manus, Bougainville and western New Guinea. They cannot be a border for one government, people or language family. Archaeology instead reveals many local histories. Around 1500, houses probably stood beside older drained gardens at Kuk. Gulf villages made and exchanged pottery; Massim islanders moved obsidian through village-specific connections; coastal foodways combined reef collecting, fishing, plants and domestic animals. These examples are local, and their calibrated dates are ranges rather than diary entries. A possible Portuguese visit in 1526 to 1527 belongs to western New Guinea or nearby islands outside the target shape and did not create political control. Families, craftspeople, gardeners, fishers and travelers taught skills without an island-wide school system. Evidence for remedies, water treatment, toilets and exact household rules is sparse, so this card says when it does not know. The 1530 label change is an atlas handoff. Communities, languages, lands and exchange continued.

periods.title: 1492 to 1496: a modern label appears early
periods.summary: The exact feature first appears in the 1492 file, although no reviewed source identifies a local founding in that year. Its two components are atlas geography, not a contemporary nation. This short teaching slice marks software coverage and carries no claim of synchronized political change.

periods.title: 1496 to 1500: exchange evidence stays local
periods.summary: Northern Massim obsidian patterns are archaeologically visible by 1350 to 1500, but researchers stress village-specific connections. That is evidence for skilled voyaging and social links, not one eastern New Guinea administration. The 1496 boundary only divides the required narrative into a cautious teaching interval.

periods.title: 1500 to 1505: the outline is copied with tiny shifts
periods.summary: The 1500 feature retains two components, 156 positions and every tested point membership from 1492. Its coordinate hash changes because several latitude values shift slightly. No historical source ties those sub-kilometer edits to a migration, treaty, survey or decision by communities on the ground.

periods.title: 1505 to 1510: gardens outlast invented year lines
periods.summary: Kuk Phase 5 began broadly before this interval, and archaeologists place a few houses in the wetland probably around 1500. The dating is approximate and the houses are locally specific. Nothing makes 1505 a highland turning point; the slice simply keeps the card contiguous.

periods.title: 1510 to 1515: pottery records work, not a kingdom
periods.summary: Keveoki 1 preserves a short-lived Gulf village and trade ceramics around 450 to 500 calibrated years BP, near the opening of this card. Decoration, clay and deposition illuminate craft and exchange. They do not identify every resident, an exact five-year event or island-wide authority.

periods.title: 1515 to 1521: sea roads remain plural
periods.summary: Massim archaeology reconstructs changing pottery sequences, island connections and voyaging shaped by seasonal winds and canoe performance. Those networks had different northern and southern histories. The evidence supports regional skill and exchange, while the 1515 and 1521 boundaries remain editorial divisions rather than dated local revolutions.

periods.title: 1521 to 1526: multilingual worlds need no single capital
periods.summary: Papuan and Austronesian speakers interacted through settlement, trade and exchange long before colonial rule. Contact could produce borrowing and trade languages without erasing local speech. The sources do not reveal a uniform event between 1521 and 1526, so this period foregrounds diversity and documentary silence.

periods.title: 1526 to 1530: an outsider visit remains outside the polygon
periods.summary: A government education text places Jorge de Meneses on western New Guinea while seeking a route to the Moluccas. Waigeo and the Bird's Head lie outside the target geometry. The 1530 file then replaces this id with Papuans, an atlas relabeling rather than conquest or collapse.

sections.title: Start with the anachronistic name and exact shape

items.text: The index has one exact papua-new-guinea record, one imported alias and a circa 1492 to 1530 span. Coverage lists two files and no card. The name belongs to a modern state, so this historical entry is treated as a regional umbrella and its imported state classification is corrected.

In 1492 the target is a two-component MultiPolygon with two rings, 156 positions and bounds from about 140.75 east to 152.27 east and 10.74 south to 2.79 south. Its decoded geometry SHA-256 is 7ac8da0d934625ca2d66c30fb6441d43edc75445014cf07579180b29a5087122, providing a reproducible audit fingerprint.

Port Moresby, Kuk, Mount Hagen, Tari, Goroka, Kainantu, Lae, a lower Sepik probe and Kandrian fall inside both target shapes. Wewak, Madang, Milne Bay, the Trobriands, Manus, central New Britain, Rabaul, New Ireland, Bougainville, Jayapura, Fakfak, Waigeo and Torres Strait do not.

The 1492 and 1500 geometries have identical component, ring and position counts and identical tested memberships, yet different coordinate hashes. Their bounds differ only slightly in latitude. That pattern points to basemap quantization or copying, not a thirty-year border survey with suspiciously modern precision.

At 1530 the atlas substitutes papuans-1530 and adds a large western component. By 1700 that western portion disappears; in 1715 papua-new-guinea-1715 inherits the exact reduced geometry. These relabelings support separate cards and careful comparison, not one institution lasting from 1492 into the modern era.

sections.title: Let local evidence set the scale

items.text: New Guinea archaeology developed through changing questions, excavations and dating methods. Early researchers sometimes forced finds into simple migration stages; later work built longer local sequences. A responsible card therefore compares sites without turning one valley, coast or island into a miniature model of every community in the polygon.

Archaeological dates are usually calibrated ranges. Nimowa, for example, has one older occupation and another within the last 460 to 300 calibrated years, a span crossing this card but wider than it. A range can locate evidence near 1500; it cannot narrate what happened in a particular five-year slice.

Gadsup and Agarabi oral histories guided surveys of former settlements, while pottery chemistry tested movements and exchange in the Arona Valley. This modern collaboration shows how community knowledge and laboratory analysis can meet. It does not make every oral account a verbatim record from 1492 or every sherd a named ancestor.

Ruisasi 1 contains nearly twenty thousand sherds in one excavated square, including standardized vessel forms. Even such abundance is a deposit from one place and an earlier period, shaped by preservation and excavation. Potsherd counts reveal production and discard; they are not a census of an entire coast.

A government learning text places an early Portuguese landing on western New Guinea and describes exchange for cloth and metal tools. The target polygon begins far east of that setting. An outsider voyage can illuminate regional contact, but it cannot serve as a first meeting for every community or a deed of sovereignty.

sections.title: Grow, gather, fish and cook in many environments

items.text: Microfossils at Kuk show ancient exploitation of banana and taro and much older cultivation than this card. They establish deep highland plant knowledge, not a menu frozen until 1500. Different elevations and coasts supported other foods, and preserved starch cannot tell us each household's recipe, portion or meal schedule.

Kuk Phase 5 combined drained garden plots with sparse houses probably late in the phase around 1500. Stone fragments and a grinding or pounding tool occur in mixed phase contexts. The evidence supports cultivation and maintenance work while leaving crop proportions, ownership and daily routines uncertain.

Last-millennium deposits around Madang contain shellfish, reef fish, birds, pigs or perhaps dogs, plant traces in dental calculus and starch residues in pottery. That varied foodway belongs to a northeastern coastal network. It should not be copied into highland gardens, Gulf villages or every year from 1492 to 1530.

Ruisasi's residents exploited several marine environments and left a dense pottery midden. The occupation predates this card by centuries, so it demonstrates an older south-coast tradition rather than an exact 1500 meal. Marine specialists still farmed knowledge: tides, habitats, tools and cooking all required practiced timing.

Claims about early pigs and pottery in Melanesia have repeatedly changed when old contexts were redated. That debate matters for daily life: finding a bone or sherd does not automatically prove husbandry or cooking practice in 1500. The card keeps pigs possible in local economies without declaring one universal pig system.

sections.title: Move pottery, stone and stories over water

items.text: Keveoki 1 was a short-lived settlement on a former beach ridge near the Vailala River. Its decorated ceramics help date the recipient end of hiri-related exchange around 1450 to 1500. The village shows coastal movement and craft circulation, not a single trade organization governing the whole Gulf.

Obsidian from Massim sites was chemically matched to different Fergusson sources. Northern Kula connections are visible by 1350 to 1500, while later southern relationships developed differently. The result is almost the opposite of an atlas blob: individual villages maintained particular links rather than obeying one uniform network.

Nimowa's Malakai site yielded pottery, shell, stone and a primary burial, with a later occupation spanning roughly 1490 to 1650. Decorative continuity accompanied more vessel forms. This locates one Louisiade community near the target interval while reminding us that island exchange and mainland histories were not interchangeable.

Vitiaz Strait archaeology follows pottery style and clay, obsidian quantities, shell, bone and animal remains across sites linking the mainland and Bismarcks. Exchange moved useful goods without requiring centralized government. Each material travels differently, so archaeologists reconstruct routes from several clues rather than drawing one all-purpose arrow.

Massim voyaging depended on seasonal winds and the sailing performance of particular canoes. Archaeology can trace pottery and island links, but hulls and sails preserve poorly. Calling people skilled navigators is well supported; assigning every island the same canoe design, crew structure or departure calendar in 1500 is not.

sections.title: Build homes, families and social ties cautiously

items.text: A few Kuk houses probably stood in the swamp around 1500, amid a long-managed garden landscape. Their scarcity partly reflects visibility and excavation strategy. Houses show residence near work, but the postholes do not announce who slept together, who owned plots or whether one household pattern covered the highlands.

Later Wahgi observations distinguish family houses, men's houses and women's houses, sometimes with space for pigs. Archaeological ditches and floors can be compared with those forms, but the source itself warns through variation and rebuilding. A twentieth-century floor plan is not a ready-made blueprint for a 1500 household.

Massim obsidian connections were village-specific, and some later patterns tracked kinship partners over generations. That shows social relationships could move material. It does not license an atlas-wide family tree, and the strongest named kin connections in the study postdate 1500, so the card keeps their chronology visible.

Gulf oral traditions describe inter-family hiri partnerships and, in some cases, temporary adoption that strengthened exchange. These accounts were recorded much later and concern named coastal relationships. They reveal social possibilities, not a universal sixteenth-century rule about marriage, adoption, inheritance or who counted as family.

A primary burial at Nimowa places care for the dead within a settled island landscape near this broad period. Pottery, shell and stone accompanied the site's history, but one burial cannot reconstruct mourning words, kin categories or status rules. Respect begins by refusing to make the individual an anonymous cultural mascot.

sections.title: Watch children learn without inventing schools

items.text: Teeth from late prehistoric Nebira and Motupore preserve enamel defects used as nonspecific signs of childhood stress. The two communities show different patterns, and their broad 850 to 200 years BP range crosses many generations. The evidence can discuss childhood health locally, not name a cause or describe every child's experience in 1500.

Australian Museum research records stone-tool learning through observation, practice, correction and material choice in much later highland communities. It offers a careful analogy for how complex hand skills can be taught without classrooms. It does not prove the same lesson sequence, age grades or teachers existed in 1492.

Ruisasi's standardized globular pots imply repeated technical choices in clay preparation, shaping and firing. Someone had to learn those choices, yet archaeology does not identify a school, a child's first pot or whether instruction used demonstration, stories or correction. Skill transmission is supported; a curriculum is not.

Arona Valley research lets oral histories choose survey locations and then compares local and imported pottery through chemistry. That is education in evidence as well as evidence about the past. It also shows why named community knowledge should guide interpretation instead of being squeezed into an outsider's single migration story.

No school building, island-wide curriculum or 1492 lesson timetable appears in the reviewed Kuk, coastal or island archaeology. Children likely learned language, food work, routes and craft through social life, but exact ages and roles remain unknown. The honest classroom here is evidence with its hand raised.

sections.title: Recognize technical achievements without a state

items.text: Wanelek pottery includes one vessel made from northeast-coast material and others made inland, showing highland participation in wider technological histories long before 1500. Pottery, polished axes and slate tools were not signs of one civilization marching uphill. They record selective adoption, local manufacture and exchange across difficult terrain.

Pottery around Madang can be studied as a process linking clay, temper, forming, firing, exchange, use and discard. Makers and materials shaped one another over time. That approach values technical judgment without pretending a pot style equals an ethnic border or that every household made its own vessels.

Geochemical work on New Britain tools distinguishes flaked, dressed and ground stone and traces movement within and beyond the island. A tool's chemistry can reveal source connections even when a maker's name is lost. The achievement lies in material knowledge and exchange, not in forcing objects into modern provinces.

Mailu research compares where settlements sat, which environmental zones they used, where clay originated and how pottery moved. Those linked decisions could make a place important without turning it into a capital. Centrality in one exchange landscape is not the same thing as rule over the atlas polygon.

At Nimowa, later deposits contain more vessel forms while decorative motifs show continuity. Innovation and continuity can coexist, which is more interesting than an old-versus-new cartoon. The sequence belongs to one southern Massim island and warns against calling any single pottery tradition the art style of Papua New Guinea.

sections.title: Discuss health, medicine and care without prescriptions

items.text: Nebira and Motupore teeth show different combinations of cavities, calculus, tooth loss, lesions and childhood enamel defects. Researchers connect these patterns cautiously to diet, ecology and stress. A skeleton records biological outcomes, not a complete diagnosis, remedy or healer's explanation, and the samples represent two communities only.

A modern East Sepik survey documents highly varied medicinal plants, plant parts, preparations and uses among four language areas. That diversity is the lesson for this card. It proves neither that a listed remedy existed in 1500 nor that one medical tradition covered the Sepik, highlands and islands.

Madang remains show reef foods, terrestrial animals, palms, betelnut, banana and cooked starches. Diverse food access could support health, but archaeological residues cannot reveal portion size, hunger seasons or who received scarce foods. Foodways matter medically without becoming a claim that diet was equal or always sufficient.

The modern East Sepik medicinal survey records different plants, plant parts and preparations in neighboring language areas, and it also notes the need for clinical testing. That double caution matters historically: local knowledge was specific, while neither modern use nor laboratory promise can identify a sixteenth-century prescription.

No reviewed source supports an island-wide hospital, physician class, pharmacy or standard birth procedure for 1492 to 1530. That absence does not mean people lacked skilled care. Archaeology preserves teeth, tools and deposits more readily than touch, spoken advice, plant knowledge or a helper's calm judgment.

Kuk's drains managed wetland water for cultivation across long phases. They required planning and maintenance, but they were field infrastructure, not drinking-water pipes or sewers. Calling them sophisticated is accurate; turning every ditch into sanitation would be the archaeological equivalent of mistaking a garden hose for indoor plumbing.

Keveoki stood on a former coastal ridge, where river, sea and rainfall shaped settlement possibilities. The report explains ceramics and village duration, not a universal water-treatment rule. People plainly managed daily water needs, but no secure source here identifies one 1500 boiling, filtering, storage or washing routine.

Ruisasi's marine specialists knew several coastal habitats, while their pottery midden records discard beside village life. Neither fish bones nor broken pots reveal where drinking water was drawn or how waste was separated. Environmental expertise is visible; an exact household sanitation plan remains beyond the deposit.

The reviewed Vitiaz and Mailu studies describe settlements, pottery, clay, food remains, shell, bone and exchange, but no securely dated 1492 to 1530 toilet, latrine, sewer or night-soil system. That is a negative finding about evidence, not a claim that people ignored cleanliness or waste.

Ordinary waste often survives as scattered bone, shell, ash and sherds, while leaves, wood and cleaning routines decay. Archaeologists can study middens without finding a bathroom blueprint. So the toilet answer is unknown, gently but firmly: history left many pots, yet none arrived with a flush-handle label.

sections.title: Keep many languages, cautious encounters and continuity

items.text: Papuan and Austronesian languages met through trade, settlement and movement, sometimes producing borrowing or trade varieties. Papuan is not one language family, and modern language maps cannot simply be pasted onto 1500. Multilingual skill itself was an achievement, especially where exchange partners needed relationships across speech boundaries.

Written-language sample: none securely attributable to communities inside the exact target polygon during 1492 to 1530 was found. A Portuguese report or Malay place-name would be outsider evidence, not community-authored writing. Later alphabets are valuable records, but printing one here as a 1500 local quotation would invent a witness.

Motu received an early missionary-designed spelling system and a school publication in 1877, more than three centuries after this card. That secure date explains the restraint: a modern or nineteenth-century Motu phrase cannot fill a sixteenth-century sample box, even though spoken languages and oral knowledge were rich.

The Portuguese voyage belongs to a written imperial archive, and the government education account places the landing in western New Guinea. It records an encounter, not the voices of every person encountered. The target excludes Waigeo and the Bird's Head, so even the atlas association must remain explicitly uncertain.

In 1530 this id disappears and papuans-1530 appears with a broader westward shape. In 1715 another Papua New Guinea id inherits a reduced eastern outline. No community fell at either seam. Languages, gardens, travel, family relations and exchange continued while atlas categories changed names and components.

ending.text: At 1530 the atlas removes papua-new-guinea and introduces the separate papuans-1530 record with a broader western component. No people, language or government fell at that software seam. Communities across eastern New Guinea and nearby islands continued their own histories, while later atlas labels changed shape again. This card therefore records continuity, leaves fell null and names no automatic successor.
